nm_south_southeast_right_face.blurb: The far right side of the Enchanted Tower, a steep roadless-feeling wedge up at roughly 8,000 feet near Datil. All eleven routes here are bolted sport lines, and the grade spread is serious: a couple of 5.11s, the bulk in the 5.12s, and a handful of 5.13s. This is the hard end of the tower, with Golden Stairs as the usual first taste before the climbs get much harder. Expect overhanging rock rather than gentle slabs. The face picks up the sun in the morning during fall and winter, then slips into shade fairly early on summer days, which makes it a pleasant choice when the tower's other faces are baking.

nm_candy_store_the.blurb: A basalt cliff rising from the bank of the Rio Grande in the Wild and Scenic stretch north of Questa. It is mainly a trad crag: ten of its eleven lines want a rack, with one bolted route, and the grades run from the low 5.10s through 5.11 with a single 5.12. The draw is clean splitter cracks and corners on hard rock, with anchors on top for lowering. This is a remote, adventurous day rather than a roadside stop: you descend to the river, walk upstream and cross the water, and you finish with a stiff climb back out. Mornings and evenings are most comfortable, and fall is considered the best time. Watch for poison ivy near the water.

nm_06_the_dihedral_wall.blurb: One of a dozen walls along the upper cliff band at Palomas Peak, in the Sandia foothills near Placitas outside Albuquerque. It holds eleven routes, a mix of mostly bolted sport lines and a few trad climbs, from 5.9 up through three 5.12s, with the middle grades evenly represented. Although the name suggests dihedrals, not every line follows one; the standouts are the two best-known corner routes. The limestone here is sharp and textured, so expect edging, smearing and small holds, and tape up for the cracks. The wall sits a short way past another named sector and has a pile of broken boulders at its base. Lowering hardware is in place on every route.
